To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cholesterol content of liposomes is a key factor in determining the extent to which liposomes remain stable in vivo and in the presence of blood, plasma or sera.
the stability of liposomes, i.e. their resistance to leakage of their aqueous contents, is controlled by their cholesterol content.

liposomes with a high cholesterol content remain stable in the circulation, in whole blood, plasma, serum or stored at low temperature for long periods of time, whereas liposomes with a low cholesterol content are rapidly destabilized in vivo and in blood, plasma, or serum in vitro, and are rapidly destroyed when stored at 4°C.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of the cholesterol content on the stability of small unil lamellar neutral, positively and negatively charged liposomes.
the stability of liposomes composed of various phospholipids and cholesterol.
the development of liposomes that are stable in vivo and in the blood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cholesterol-rich liposomes (i.e. those with a molar ratio of egg phosphatidylocholine/cholestrol of 7:7) are the most stable liposomes in biological systems in vitro and in vivo.
cholesterol-rich liposomes are stable in vivo and in the blood, plasma or in the presence of serum, and that cholesterol-free and/or cholesterol-poor liposomes are not stable.
liposomal stability is a complex function of the lipid composition and the biological system in which the liposomes are present.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cholesterol-rich liposomes are stable in blood and serum in vitro and in vivo.

cholesterol-rich liposomes are very stable, cholesterol-poor liposomes are very unstable, cholesterol-free liposomes are very, very unstable, and that cholesterol-rich liposome are the most promising for in vivo and in-vitro use.
liposomes with cholesterol content of about 40% (w/w) are stable in blood and in plasma, but not in serum.
The main takeaway from our work is that

liposomal stability can be controlled by adjusting the cholesterol content of the liposome bilayer, and that this is an important factor to be considered in designing liposomes to be used as drug carriers in biological systems.
liposomes with a cholesterol content above a critical threshold remain stable in vivo and in the presence of plasma or whole blood.

cholesterol-rich liposomes are more stable in vivo and in the presence of blood than are cholesterol-poor or cholesterol-free liposomes, regardless whether the liposomes are neutral, negatively charged or positively charged.
